name: Nikhil Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for an electrical wholesaler that supplies contractors: cable drums, switchgear, sockets, LED panels, that kind of thing. My day is mostly checking stock levels against what the branches are selling, raising purchase orders, and arguing with suppliers about lead times. Copper prices swing every week, so a lot of it is deciding when to buy cable and how much.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI fit in at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then I'll paste a long supplier spec sheet into a chatbot and ask it to pull out the bits I need, or tidy up an email. It's useful, but I check everything, because once it told me a breaker was rated for the wrong current. I'm not against it; I just wait to see it work before I lean on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more or less what I see today, so it doesn't feel like a big change. A few shortcuts, same job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's a handy helper, not a revolution. I'd probably post that the money should have gone into wages and training instead of hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine about my own job. Copper buying needs judgement and phone calls, and contractors want someone who picks up. What bothers me is that pay at our place is flat and the owners keep talking about margins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chatbot for spec sheets and nothing more. I'd keep saving about two hundred a month, since Leo and I want a deposit for a flat in three or four years. And I'd keep nudging colleagues to join the union, which only half of us are in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of frustration about pay, but that's ordinary life, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Leo think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo teaches at a secondary school, so Leo hears about AI mostly as kids cheating on homework. Leo would say the same thing: it's a tool, so use it and stop panicking. We're both pretty level about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work this would still hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The girl on the returns desk spends her day matching credit notes to invoices. That's exactly the routine stuff even a plateau AI would take. I'd want her moved into something else before anyone talks about cutting the role.

say: AI is a **handy helper**, not a revolution.
The money should go into **wages and training** instead of hype.
think: My **copper buying** needs judgement and phone calls, so my job is safe.
Flat **pay** while owners talk margins bothers me more than AI.
do: Keep using the **chatbot** for spec sheets only.
Save about **200 a month** toward a flat deposit with Leo.
S0.quote: Copper buying needs judgement and phone calls, and contractors want someone who picks up.
fieldNote: Nikhil treats the plateau as **today's reality**, so it barely moves him.
His concern shifts to **colleagues in routine roles**, like the returns desk.
Saving for a **flat deposit** with Leo is his main money goal.

steps.text: Keep using the chatbot only to read supplier spec sheets
Save about 200 a month toward a flat deposit
Ask two warehouse colleagues to join the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we're talking about my actual job. Buying and checking and planning, that's every hour of my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan, agreed with staff, about which tasks go to software and what happens to the people. I'd post that productivity gains should be shared, not just banked by shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the company would cut buyers. There are five of us across the branches, and one person with good software could probably do the routine reordering for all of them. I'd want to be the one running the software, not the one who gets let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for training on the new tools as soon as they're announced, and I'd do an online course in supply chain analytics on weekends. I'd hold off on the flat deposit for a year until I see how the cuts fall. And I'd get the union rep to ask for a no-redundancy promise in exchange for us learning the new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. I'm not frozen, I'm just aware the chairs are being taken away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wait to see things proven. Is that still true here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that worries me. If I wait until it's proven, someone else has already learned it. So I'd have to move earlier than I'm comfortable with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our oldest buyer, who has been there twenty-six years and does everything on paper. My colleague knows every supplier by first name, but that won't count if a manager is looking at a spreadsheet of costs.

say: We need a **plan agreed with staff** about which tasks go to software.
**Productivity gains** should be shared, not banked by shareholders.
think: The company would likely **cut buyers** from five to fewer.
I want to be **running the software**, not the one let go.
do: Ask my manager for **training** as soon as tools are announced.
Take a weekend course in **supply chain analytics**.
Delay the **flat deposit** for a year until cuts are clear.
feel: Aware the **chairs are being taken** away.
S1.quote: There are five of us across the branches, and one person with good software could probably do the routine reordering for all of them.
fieldNote: Nikhil sees the card as describing **his whole week**, and shifts quickly from calm to worried.
He admits his **wait-and-see habit** is a liability here and would move earlier.
He links learning the tools to a **union bargain** on redundancy.

steps.text: Ask the manager for training when the new buying tools arrive
Take a weekend online course in supply chain analytics
Put the flat deposit on hold for a year
Ask the union rep to seek a no-redundancy promise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. That's two copper cycles. I wouldn't even finish a course in that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political emergency, not a tech story. I'd be online calling for income support and a shorter working week, so the gains get spread out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think buying as a job just ends. Everything I do is thinking work: forecasts, orders, negotiations by email. The only hands-on part is the odd visit to the warehouse, so the extra three years before robots doesn't help me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the flat and keep the cash liquid. I'd look at moving into the electrical trade itself, maybe an apprenticeship as an electrician, because I know the products and robots for that come about three years later. And I'd join a campaign for basic income straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Like the ground's gone soft. I'd be twenty-nine and starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship at twenty-nine, on lower pay. Could you afford it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only just, with Leo's salary. We'd move somewhere cheaper, probably back near my parents. Leo would hate the commute but Leo's job is safer than mine in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And in 2031 when robots arrive for the hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. Maybe the electrician gets three good years. But wiring old houses is messy and odd, so maybe longer. In this picture, I'd be betting my career on the messy wiring jobs that robots find hardest.

say: This is a **political emergency**, not a tech story.
We need **income support** and a shorter working week.
think: Buying as a job **just ends** within two years.
The robot delay doesn't help, because my work is almost all **thinking work**.
do: Stop saving for the flat and keep **cash liquid**.
Start an **electrician apprenticeship**, using what I know about the products.
feel: **Scared**, like the ground has gone soft.
S2.quote: In this picture, I'd be betting my career on the messy wiring jobs that robots find hardest.
fieldNote: Nikhil quickly sees **no shelter** in the robot delay for a desk-based buyer.
He'd pivot to the **electrical trade**, a hands-on move built on product knowledge.
Partner Leo's **safer income** becomes the household anchor.

steps.text: Move flat savings into an easy-access account
Apply for an electrician apprenticeship with a local contractor
Move somewhere cheaper near his parents
Join a campaign group calling for basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to do something. Not enough to be relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a short window to shape this, and I'd be pushing the union and local politicians to set up retraining funds before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see the buying job as a five-year contract. I'd use the AI tools hard in the meantime, because the person who gets the most out of them keeps their job longest. Then I'd want to be in something hands-on or in a role where people trust a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn the new buying tools properly and get good at them. I'd start an evening electrical course in the second year, so by 2031 I'm qualified. And I'd keep the flat deposit going but smaller, about a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but organised. It's a deadline I can plan around, which is better than a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you only use AI now and then. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deadline changes it. If I know the buying job is ending, then squeezing it for five more years means using the tools every day. It's not love, it's survival.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leo we still buy, but smaller and later, and somewhere cheaper. I don't want to give up on a home because of a forecast, but I don't want a big mortgage on a job with an end date either.

say: We have a **short window** to shape this.
Unions and politicians should set up **retraining funds** before 2031.
think: I'd treat my buying job as a **five-year contract** with a fixed end.
Whoever uses the **AI tools** best keeps the job longest.
do: Learn the new **buying tools** properly in year one.
Start an **evening electrical course** in year two.
Cut the **flat deposit** savings to about 100 a month.
feel: Glad of a **deadline** rather than a wall.
S3.quote: If I know the buying job is ending, then squeezing it for five more years means using the tools every day. It's not love, it's survival.
fieldNote: Five years turns Nikhil from an occasional AI user into a **daily one**, out of necessity.
He plans a **two-track** path: the tools now, the electrical trade later.
He keeps the **home plan** but shrinks it, a steady person's hedge.

steps.text: Learn the company's new buying software in the first year
Start an evening electrical installation course in year two
Cut flat deposit saving to about 100 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole second career's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to plan properly as a society, with public training and fair rules. No excuses for chaos with ten years' notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect buying to disappear, but I'd have time to choose where to land. I'd probably go into energy work, like installing heat pumps and solar, which is hands-on and in demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in buying for now and use the tools as they prove themselves. In year two I'd start a part-time electrical qualification. And I'd keep saving for the flat at the normal pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned but hopeful. It's far enough away that I can make it a choice instead of a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make it easier to wait and see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, and that's the danger with me. I'd tell myself there's loads of time, then suddenly it's year seven. So I'd set myself a date to start the course and stick to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the energy move work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A government grant for training, and an employer willing to take a thirty-year-old apprentice. Leo's already said Leo would support it if we planned it.

say: Ten years is a **chance to plan** properly as a society.
There's **no excuse for chaos** with that much notice.
think: Buying will still **disappear**, but I can choose where to land.
I'd likely move into **heat pumps and solar**.
do: Stay in buying and use tools **as they prove** themselves.
Start a **part-time electrical** qualification in year two.
Keep saving for the **flat** at the normal pace.
feel: Glad it can be a **choice** rather than a scramble.
S4.quote: I'd tell myself there's loads of time, then suddenly it's year seven.
fieldNote: Nikhil still expects to **lose buying work**, but the long runway gives him agency.
He spots his own **procrastination** risk and sets himself a hard date.
His ideal landing is **green energy installation**, hands-on and in demand.

steps.text: Keep buying and adopt tools once they prove themselves
Start a part-time electrical qualification in year two
Keep saving 200 a month toward the flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is too short for anyone in a desk job to switch to anything real. What would help is paid retraining with an income while you do it, and employers being made to take on older apprentices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the suppliers. If every distributor uses the same AI to buy, small suppliers who rely on a good relationship get squeezed out. That's a quiet loss nobody talks about.

headlineQuote: If every distributor uses the same AI to buy, small suppliers who rely on a good relationship get squeezed out.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old buyer** at an electrical wholesaler, living with Leo, a teacher.
He uses AI **now and then** but waits to see things proven before relying on them.
He's **progressive**, pro-union and sees AI gains as something to share fairly.
He moves from calm to **alarmed** as timelines shorten, eyeing the electrical trade as a landing.
With ten years he plans a **green energy** career and guards against his own procrastination.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to switch from desk work.
whatWouldHelp: Employers made to take on **older apprentices**.
